summary:
Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. The national framework binds Lima directly: the Congress that enacted these measures sits and operates in the capital, and its provisions apply throughout the department and the metropolitan area.

On 2 April 2025 the Plenary of Congress approved, exempt from a second vote, the fused bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR, promulgated as the April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents. Article 5 prohibits entry to and use of public sanitary facilities by any person whose biological sex does not match the sex for which the facility is designated, with listed exceptions, barring trans people including trans youth from facilities matching their gender identity. The provision followed a February 2025 unanimous approval by the Congress Women and Family Commission of the Muñante initiative presented by Jorge Montoya of Honor y Democracia, which still required plenary backing at that point. The same text bars inclusive signage, including the wording the international airport Jorge Chávez in Lima had installed, reading "for all persons with female identity" and "male identity", and the wider package bans signage of the kind "women in their diversity".

Enforcement of the restriction reaches private and public life. LGBTIQ activist Gianna Camacho, co-author of a 2024 report on hate crimes and a trans journalist and human-rights defender, states that the rule would reduce to security staff demanding a DNI on their own judgement of whether a woman entering a restroom is trans. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to "go use the men's room".

The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, analysing the text on 15 April 2025, calls article 5 direct legislation conditioning basic rights on a "biological sex" and a violation of the equality and non-discrimination principle, and finds the rule openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by implicitly framing them as harassment risks. IDEHPUCP also recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The TLGBI Rights Observatory annual report, covered on 22 July 2024, recorded 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 reports of rights violations between 2020 and 2023; more than half of the dead were trans women (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. The year 2023 saw the most homicides (19), and no suspects were identified in 26 of the 54 killings. The same reporting states that hate crimes in Peru are rising with trans women most affected, and Camacho stresses that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. Peru has no official system recording victims' sexual orientation, and hate crimes go unsanctioned.

Lima has seen lethal anti-trans violence: on 12 February 2023 the transgender sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, aged 31, was kidnapped from jirón Chancay in central Lima by the "Los Gallegos" extortion gang, who killed her with roughly 30 gunshots.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.
tangentialFactors:
Peru's position on hate-crime coverage is unusual in its subregion: it is one of only three South American states, alongside Paraguay and Guyana, whose hate-crime law carries no LGBT anti-discrimination coverage after the 2017 Penal Code repeal.

The Inter-American system has engaged Peru directly. Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 obliges states to guarantee trans people's full rights on the basis of protected personal autonomy, and the Azul Rojas Marín judgment is recorded as that Court's first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, routed through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Recorded figures understate the problem, in the assessment of the co-author of the 2024 hate-crime report, who describes the national counts as a sub-registry. The absence of an official system registering victims' sexual orientation is itself cited as a reason hate crimes go unsanctioned.

IDEHPUCP has documented congressional rhetoric alongside statute, including dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu, and characterises the bathroom provision as framing trans people as harassment risks while they are more often the victims of violence.
localsOnly:
Residents of Lima live under the national bathroom rule as applied to every public restroom in the department, from public offices and schools to shopping centres and transport terminals, with article 5's listed exceptions governing the narrow cases where access is permitted.

ID checks are the practical pressure point described by local activists: enforcement would rest on private security personnel deciding, on their own judgement, whether a woman presenting a DNI at a restroom is trans. A gym complaint brought by a trans woman under the policy was dismissed by the consumer-protection body.

Inclusive signage installed in Lima has been removed from scope by law, covering wording such as that used at the international airport Jorge Chávez and formulations like "women in their diversity".

Healthcare settings improved terminologically in June 2024, when health authorities struck pathologising language for gender diversity from official guidance, and a Lima constitutional court ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional in July 2025 after an activist challenge.

Homicide data specific to the capital is not separated out in the observatory figures; the national counts for 2020 to 2023 cover Lima within the national total, and the killing of Rubí Torres Silvano in central Lima in February 2023 is one documented case in which no suspects were identified.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether article 5 has been challenged before the Constitutional Court, or suspended by any Lima court, is unresolved in these sources; only the separate July 2025 ruling against an anti-equality decree is documented, and its relationship to the bathroom provision is not stated.

Whether any Lima authority has issued operational instructions for enforcing biological-sex designation in restrooms, beyond the activists' described expectation of private DNI checks, is not sourced.

Figures on the number of Lima establishments enforcing the policy, and on refusals of entry to trans people in the metropolitan area, are not available in this inventory; only the single dismissed gym complaint is on record.

The 2017 repeal's effect on specific chargeable offences in Lima, and whether prosecutors have brought any bias-related charges under other articles since then, are not covered here.

The stated one-million-signature petition behind the 2017 repeal is reported as a claim made at the time rather than an independently verified total.
